verses.translation_literal: For the leader, upon the Gittith, of Asaph.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung to the Gittith. A song of Asaph.
verses.directors_commentary: The heading is stage direction, not scripture's story, and it was already obscure to the ancient commentators. "Choirmaster" renders the same word the KJV calls "chief Musician", a Levitical overseer of the Temple music. The Gittith (also in the headings of Psalms 8 and 84) is most likely an instrument or tune "of Gath", as Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it. Ibn Ezra does not repeat himself here; he says only that he has already explained the word, which sends the reader back to his comment on Psalm 8. Do not play it as mystery; play it as the cue card pinned to the music stand: Temple, orchestra, Asaph's guild. Later tradition (Radak, Meiri) says this psalm was sung at the new year, which tells us how the congregation heard it, not what the heading itself says.

philological_notes.note: A musical term of uncertain meaning, read as an instrument or melody from Gath, the Philistine city. The same word heads Psalms 8 and 84. Ibn Ezra refers to his explanation of the word elsewhere rather than giving one here.

A piel participle, 'the one who oversees/leads', from a root that elsewhere means 'be pre-eminent, lasting'. The KJV 'chief Musician' is a fair gloss; the heading marks the piece as for the Temple choir leader.

verses.translation_literal: Shout for joy to God, our strength; shout in triumph to the God of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing! Let the whole assembly break into singing for God, our strength, and let the shout go up for the God of Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary: Two imperatives open the psalm like a conductor's two raised hands, and they are two different sounds. "Sing for joy" (רנן) is the voice; "shout" (רוע) is the war-cry and the trumpet-blast, and it is the root of תרועה, the teru'ah, the festival blast. Verse 4 will then call for the horn itself with another verb, תקע, "blow". The KJV flattens both imperatives into "sing aloud" and "make a joyful noise", which makes it sound like a choir rehearsal. The Hebrew has the whole crowd on its feet. The divine title is Elohim here, not the personal name; this is the Elohistic Psalter, and the psalm does not name YHWH until verse 11. Pair "our strength" (עֹז) with "the God of Jacob": the first is what he is to us, the second is the line of promise he belongs to. Tradition (Rashi, Radak) ties the shout to the new-year trumpet, but the verse itself only demands volume.

philological_notes.note: To raise a shout, whether for victory, for a king, or at the trumpet's blast; the same root provides תרועה, the festival 'teru'ah' blast. Metzudat David reads it here as 'with the shofar', which fits the next verses.
'Our strength', also 'refuge, fortress'. Meiri takes it as 'our stronghold', the God who showed his might in Egypt.

verses.translation_literal: Lift up a song and give a drum, a pleasant lyre with a harp.
verses.translation_dramatic: Raise the melody. Strike the drum. Let the sweet lyre ring out together with the harp.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the shout becomes an orchestra, and the order is the order of a procession: voice, percussion, strings. The verbs are physical. "Lift up" (שאו) is what you do with a load or a banner; the song is heavy and raised high. "Give" a drum (תנו) is odd English, and the KJV smooths it into "bring hither the timbrel", which invents an errand the Hebrew does not give. Radak reads the verb as "give your hand to the drum": hand it a beat; he extends the same phrase to the lyre and harp. Ibn Ezra makes a related grammatical point, that "give" serves the next words too, so that one verb governs drum, lyre and harp alike. The תֹף is a hand-frame drum, the instrument of Miriam and the women's dances in Exodus 15, which is a quiet signal that the psalm is already thinking about the Exodus. The kinnor and nevel are two different stringed instruments, not synonyms. Rashi records the ancient dispute whether they are the same, and the KJV's "psaltery" is a Greek-derived guess that has stuck. Ask the players for a plucked, bright sound; the adjective "pleasant" (נעים) is the same one used of the "sweet psalmist of Israel" in 2 Samuel 23:1.

philological_notes.note: A hand-held frame drum, played by women in celebration (Exod 15:20, Judg 11:34). Radak takes 'ותנו תוף' as 'give your hands to the drum'.
'Give', the verb that also serves 'a pleasant lyre with a harp' in the second half of the verse, as Ibn Ezra observes.

A large stringed instrument, probably a harp or lyre of the 'jar' type; Rashi preserves the rabbinic wordplay that it 'puts to shame' (מנבל) every other instrument. KJV 'psaltery' is a Greek loanword.

verses.translation_literal: Blow at the month a ram's horn, at the covering, for the day of our festival.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blow the ram's horn at the new moon, and again at the full, the moon in its covering, on the day of our feast.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the line the whole psalm turns on, and the KJV smooths over its calendar. "Blow up the trumpet" is off twice: the instrument is the shofar, a ram's horn, not a metal trumpet (that is the חצוצרה of Numbers 10), and the verb is simply "blow", with no "up". Then comes the calendar. Ḥodesh is the "month" and the new moon, the day the thin sickle first appears. Keseh is the rare word: it occurs here and, in the spelling כסא, in Proverbs 7:20, where the husband "will come home on the day of the keseh". Two readings are old. The first takes it as "covering": the Targum speaks of the month in which the moon is covered, and the ASV and BBE render "full moon". Ibn Ezra mentions that the moon "is covered" on that day, but then says his own view is that keseh means a fixed time, a known appointment, as in Proverbs 7:20. The second reading, "appointed time", is the one Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion and David give, and the one the KJV and Webster chose. Settle it in the room: either way, the horn sounds at the start of the month and again on the feast day. Remember the world that hears this. There are no printed calendars; the month starts when someone sees the light, and the horn tells the village. The Targum names the month of Tishri, and Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read the line as Rosh Hashanah; the psalm does not say so, and the performance need not either.

philological_notes.note: Either 'at the covering', the full moon (the Targum's 'month in which the moon is covered'; ASV and BBE), or 'at the appointed time' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion/David; Ibn Ezra's own view), with Prov 7:20 (כסא) as the parallel. Ibn Ezra records both: the moon 'is covered' on this day, but he prefers a fixed time.

A ram's horn, blown for alarm, assembly and festival. Distinct from the metal חצוצרה of Num 10:2, 10; Ibn Ezra notes that the Torah commands trumpets at the new moon, and that the shofar was blown too.

verses.translation_literal: For a statute for Israel it is, an ordinance of the God of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: For this is Israel's law, and a verdict that belongs to the God of Jacob.
verses.directors_commentary: The "for" (כי) gives the reason for all that noise: this is not mood, it is law. Two legal words stand side by side, חֹק and מִשְׁפָּט, and the second carries a double edge. A ḥok is a fixed, engraved rule, something enacted; a mishpat is a judgment, a verdict. The KJV's "statute" and "law" blur the pair. Ibn Ezra says they are near synonyms; Malbim, Meiri and Metzudat David hear a contrast, and later tradition makes this the day of divine judgment. Play it as an actor would: it is a decree for Israel, and it belongs to God as a judgment of his. The KJV also writes "this was a statute", slipping the verb into the past; the Hebrew has the present, "it is", so the law stands now. "The God of Jacob" repeats from verse 2 and frames the unit.

philological_notes.note: A fixed decree paired with a judgment. Malbim reads the pair as a contrast: a rule with no stated reason for Israel, but a judgment (with reasons) in God's eyes.

verses.translation_literal: A testimony in Joseph he set it, when he went out over the land of Egypt; a lip I did not know, I hear.
verses.translation_dramatic: He set it down as a witness in Joseph, on the day he went out over the land of Egypt. And there, a speech I had never known: I heard it.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest verse in the unit, and the one the KJV makes easiest by choosing. Three things to know. First, the name: not the usual Yosef but Yehosef, with the divine syllable inserted, which appears only here in the Bible. Ibn Ezra takes it as an honorific form, Joseph standing for all Israel, as in Psalm 77:16. Second, the verb "went out over" (צאת על) does not mean "went through", which is how the KJV and Webster read it. It is the language of an army or a ruler going out against or over a land. Is the subject Joseph taking command of Egypt (Gen 41:45), or God marching out against Egypt in the plagues, or Israel leaving? The commentators disagree, and the Hebrew will not say. Third, the last clause is a startling break in voice. A new "I" speaks: "a lip I did not know, I hear." The word "lip" (שפה) is "language", as in the tower of Babel. The KJV makes it a tidy relative clause, "where I heard a language that I understood not", but the Hebrew is a bare stammer: an unknown tongue, and I hear it. Rashi and Metzudat David say it is Joseph hearing Egyptian; Ibn Ezra says it is Israel, who had to learn it; Malbim hears the voice of a God not yet known. Direct the actor to pause before שפת.

philological_notes.note: The unique long form of Joseph's name, with the divine syllable. Ibn Ezra reads it as a mark of honour, and as standing for all Israel.

Literally 'a lip I did not know'. The construction is irregular (Ibn Ezra notes that a word like 'people' seems to be missing, as in 'those drinking in bowls of wine'). 'Lip' is idiomatic for 'language', as in Gen 11:1.
'Testimony, witness', the covenant word. Metzudat Zion links it to עדי, 'ornament', and Metzudat David reads the gold chain placed on Joseph's neck (Gen 41:42).

verses.translation_literal: I removed his shoulder from the burden; his palms from the basket they passed away.
verses.translation_dramatic: I lifted the load from his shoulder. His hands were set free from the basket, and they passed on.
verses.directors_commentary: Now God speaks outright, and the voice is gentle. The picture is forced labour, and it is concrete: a bent shoulder carrying a סֵבֶל, a load carried on the back (the word is used for the Egyptian taskmasters in Exodus 1:11 and 5:4-5), and the hand, the כף, "palm", with a דוּד. That last word is the one real fork in the verse. The Hebrew דוּד is a vessel, and it can be a cooking pot (1 Sam 2:14) or a carrying basket (Jer 24:2, baskets of figs). Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion and the Targum read "pot": the KJV's "pots" follows them, with Rashi's picture of slaves boiling pots for their masters, and Radak's of the whole clay-work. Ibn Ezra, the ASV, YLT and BBE read a basket for carrying. I choose "basket" because the Exodus 1:14 picture is of mud and bricks hauled to the pit, and a verb of passing away from the hands pairs best with a load the hands carry; but the other reading is old and respectable, not an error. Notice the grammar: "I removed" is God's act, while the second half is passive-sounding, "his hands passed away", so God acts on the shoulder, and the hands simply cross over to the other side. Keep the "his", which holds the whole people in one body, a single back and a single pair of hands, as Ibn Ezra reads it.

philological_notes.note: A vessel, either a cooking pot (1 Sam 2:14; Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion, the Targum) or a carrying basket (Jer 24:2; Ibn Ezra, ASV, BBE). Ibn Ezra reads the clause as the hands ceasing to make clay and bricks and to carry them in the basket. I prefer 'basket' for the brickmaking setting of Exod 1:14.
A heavy load borne on the shoulder; the related סִבְלוֹת names Israel's forced labour in Egypt (Exod 1:11; 6:6).

verses.translation_literal: In the distress you called and I rescued you; I answered you in the hiding place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: In your distress you cried out, and I tore you free. I answered you from the secret place of the thunder. And at the waters of Meribah I tried you. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: God's speech now compresses the whole story in three beats: cry, rescue, test. The first verb is vivid. חלץ is what you do when you pull a sandal off the foot or draw a soldier out of the line: the KJV's "delivered" is polite and loses the wrenching. The second, "the hiding place of thunder", is a lovely and puzzling phrase. Thunder is the voice of the storm god, and in the cultures around Israel it is the voice of Baal and Hadad. Here it is God's, and it is hidden, a place where the storm waits before it breaks. Rashi says the people called in secret and God answered in the open; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David place the thunder at the sea. Note the tense switch, from perfect to imperfect: the KJV's "I answered" and "I proved" turn it all into the past. The Hebrew is more open, and Meiri reads the imperfect as standing for the past. The last beat is the sting. "Meribah" means "quarrel", and the verb "test" (בחן) is the assayer's word for refining metal. The same chapter that opens in celebration now shows Israel on the testing floor, and the Selah is a pause for the audience to realize it. One note on the pointing of אבחנך: Radak reads the ח with a qamets ḥatuf, a short o, like אזכרך in Psalm 42:7; Meiri reports that some grammarians read it so and others with a full qamets.

philological_notes.note: 'The hiding place of thunder', the cloud from which the storm speaks. Rashi reads it as God's public answer to Israel's secret cry; Ibn Ezra takes it as the cloud and fire at the sea.
'I tested you', the verb for assaying metal. Radak reads the ח with a qamets ḥatuf (short o); Meiri says some grammarians read it so and others with a full qamets.
'Quarrel'; the place where Israel contended with God for water (Exod 17:7; Num 20:13). Ibn Ezra links it to the rock, where the place was named Massah and Meribah.

verses.translation_literal: Hear, my people, and let me bear witness against you; Israel, if you would listen to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen, my people, and I will give my warning. Israel, if only you would listen to me.
verses.directors_commentary: The courtroom opens. "Hear" is the first word of the Shema, and here it is God who says it. The next verb, ואעידה, is a legal one: it means "I will call witnesses" or "I will warn formally", as one gives a solemn caution before a trial. The KJV's "testify unto thee" can sound like a speech of praise; Metzudat Zion says it is the warning given before witnesses, and the preposition "in/against you" (בך) points the same way. Then the sentence "if you would listen to me" has two possible shapes, and the verse does not choose. Read as a wish, it breaks off with no result clause: the ASV's "if… !" and the BBE's "if you will only" catch the longing of a parent. Read as a condition that continues, as Radak, Malbim and Metzudat David do and as the KJV's semicolon implies, it is the opening of the next verses: if you listen, then no strange god among you, and so on, and the mouth open wide to be filled. Both are defensible. My dramatic layer plays the wish; let the actor decide how long to hold the silence. Notice also the double address: "my people" is the voice of belonging, "Israel" the voice of the covenant partner.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil cohortative of the root for 'witness': 'let me testify, let me give formal warning'. Metzudat Zion explains it as the warning given before witnesses.

A conditional that either breaks off as a wish, 'if only you would listen' (ASV, BBE), or continues into the next verses as the condition for the promise (Radak, Malbim, Metzudat David; KJV's semicolon).

verses.translation_literal: There shall not be among you a strange god, and you shall not bow down to a foreign god.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let there be no strange god among you. You shall bow to no foreign god.
verses.directors_commentary: The warning is the first commandment, almost word for word (Exodus 20:3-5), and it is spoken at the exact moment of the feast. The verbs are two: "be" among you, and "bow down". The first is a ban on having any such god around, an idol in the house or the heart; the second is a ban on worship. The KJV's "strange" for זר is a Jacobean word, and in modern English it makes the gods sound odd. The Hebrew means "alien, outside", the stranger who does not belong to the household, and נכר is the foreigner. So the pair "strange/foreign" is not synonyms for oddness but a double claim: a god from outside, a god of outsiders. The preposition בך, "in you", is notable: not "before you" but inside, which is why Meiri and the rabbis heard an inner voice, the "strange god in the body", the evil impulse. The psalm's world has actual rival gods, Baal and Asherah, within walking distance, and the line is a polemic against them.

philological_notes.note: 'A strange/alien god'. The adjective זר describes what is outside the household; בך means 'in you', so the rabbis (via Meiri) read an inner strange god, the evil impulse.
'You shall bow down in worship', the Hishtaphel stem of the root.

verses.translation_literal: I am YHWH your God, who brought you up from the land of Egypt. Open wide your mouth and I will fill it.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am the LORD your God, the one who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the preamble to the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2), spoken again, with a startling addition. In the middle of the covenant formula, the personal name YHWH finally enters the psalm after the generic "God" of the opening verses. The KJV's "brought thee out" misses the verb, which is "brought up" (העלה), the vertical word of the Exodus: Egypt is a low place, the land is up. Then comes the surprise. After all the law, the command is not a prohibition but an invitation: "widen your mouth". It is the picture of a nestling with its beak open. The KJV's "open thy mouth wide" is correct, but BBE's "so that I may give you food" supplies a meal the Hebrew does not name. What the mouth is opened for is read two ways. Rashi, Radak (on verse 9), Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra take it as asking: ask of me whatever your heart desires. Meiri and the Targum take it as learning: Meiri says "prepare yourself to learn and to know", and the Targum says "open your mouth with words of Torah", though Meiri also gives the asking reading and calls the first the main one. Ancient hearers would also have heard a polemic: the gods of Egypt and Canaan promised the fertility of the land, and here YHWH offers it in person.

philological_notes.note: 'Make your mouth wide.' Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take it as asking of God all one's heart's desire; Meiri as 'prepare yourself to learn', and the Targum as 'in the words of the Torah'.
'The one who brought you up', a hiphil participle with the article, in the formula of Exod 20:2 and Lev 11:45; Egypt is spoken of as 'down'.

verses.translation_literal: And my people did not listen to my voice, and Israel did not yield to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: But my people would not listen to my voice. Israel would not yield to me.
verses.directors_commentary: The invitation hangs in the air, and the answer is two flat clauses, one for each of the two names God has used: "my people" and "Israel". The parallelism is deliberate and it is a charge. The first verb, שמע, "listen", is the verb God has been begging for since verse 9, and its repetition here closes the loop: "hear" at the beginning of God's speech, "did not hear" here. The second verb is the sharper one. אבה means "to be willing, to consent"; it is used almost always in the negative ("would not"), and it is the language of a stubborn refusal. The KJV's "would none of me" is a good, if antique, rendering, and it captures the idiom of rejection, someone who will have none of you. Radak sets the date wide, from the wilderness to the end of the monarchy; Malbim and Meiri read the next verse's "I sent them away" as the immediate consequence. Play it quietly. After the joy of the first verses, this is the hinge to grief.

philological_notes.note: 'To be willing, to consent', found mostly in negative sentences ('was not willing'). Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion gloss it 'did not want'.

verses.translation_literal: And I sent him away in the stubbornness of their heart; they walk in their counsels.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I let go of the hand I had held. I sent him out into the stubbornness of his own heart, and he went. Down every road his own counsel drew, he went, and no voice of mine was in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm: God, who has just pleaded in v.12 that Israel would not listen, now does the thing a rejected parent does and lets go. The verb is the one used for releasing a slave or sending away a wife; it is not violence, it is a withdrawal of restraint. The sentence is said with sorrow, not with anger.

The KJV's 'unto their own hearts' lust' is the most misleading rendering in the verse. The Hebrew שרירות is not lust, which would be a desire, but stubbornness, the hardness of a will that has set itself; Jeremiah uses the same noun for 'the stubbornness of their evil heart' (Jer 3:17). 'Counsels' (מועצות) are plans, policy, the deliberation of people who think they know best. The point is that Israel gets what it chose: its own counsel in place of God's. Note also the shift from singular 'him' to plural 'their heart', which the commentators read as the nation speaking as one person and as many.

philological_notes.note: 'Stubbornness', hardness of will, not 'lust' as in the KJV. Rashi connects it with the root of 'my watchers' (Ps 5:9) in the sense of 'what the heart sees'; Ibn Ezra connects it with שריר, 'firm'. I follow the second.
Piel of 'send': to send away, release, let go. Radak reads it as God removing his guard from them; Metzudat David reads it as exile.

verses.translation_literal: If only my people [were] listening to me, Israel in my ways they would walk.
verses.translation_dramatic: If only. If only my people would listen to me. If only Israel would walk in my ways.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice breaks. After the cold sentence of v.13 comes the wish that the whole psalm has been leading to: not a threat but a longing. Play it quietly, not as an accusation. The Hebrew particle לוּ is the word for wishes that may not come true ('if only', 'would that'); it carries regret.

The KJV's 'had hearkened' makes it purely past, a verdict on what Israel failed to do, while the participle 'listening' in the Hebrew is open and present: even now the door is not shut, as Meiri observes. The phrase 'my people' is not a legal term here but a possessive of affection; the same speaker who has just sent them away still calls them his. Note the symmetry with v.13: 'they walk in their counsels' against 'they would walk in my ways', the same verb, the opposite road.

philological_notes.note: The optative particle, 'if only'; Metzudat Zion compares it with the conditional use in Judg 8:19. It expresses a wish, often an unrealized one.
Piel imperfect, 'walk about, conduct themselves'; it answers 'they walk' (v.13, Qal) and Ibn Ezra reads the pair as deliberate opposites.

verses.translation_literal: As a little, their enemies I will subdue, and against their adversaries I will turn my hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: In a little while, hardly a breath, I would bring their enemies low, and against those who pressed them I would turn my hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The promise is of speed: 'in a little while'. In the ancient Near East a king who defeated the enemies of his people was a king worth following, and the covenant God here offers what a suzerain offers a loyal vassal: protection. The point is that Israel had no need of its own counsels.

The KJV 'I should soon have subdued' is accurate, but its past conditional makes the offer sound closed. Note the phrase 'turn my hand', a gesture of striking; the Hebrew picture is of a hand that has been resting and is now brought around. Radak and Meiri take the word 'kimeat' as a true kaph of time ('like a little'), as in 'swear to me this day' (Gen 25:33), so that the sense is not 'almost' but 'in a short span'. The two words for enemies, 'oyevim' and 'tsarim', are a pair: the enemy who hates and the oppressor who presses.

philological_notes.note: 'In a little while'. Radak and Meiri take the prefixed kaph as a true kaph of time, and Ibn Ezra glosses it 'in a short time'. This is not the adverb 'almost' that the same word can be.
Literally 'return my hand': the hand is brought back to strike. Radak adds that it means striking again and again.

verses.translation_literal: Haters of YHWH would cringe to him, and may their time be for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Those who hate the LORD would cringe before him, feigning what they never felt, and their time would run on and on for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn is from Israel's enemies to the LORD's enemies: the two are the same people seen from two sides. The verb יכחשו is a Piel of 'lie', and with ל it means 'to cringe, to fawn', to give feigned submission under duress. It is the word of Ps 18:45 ('strangers shall feign obedience to me'). The KJV 'submitted themselves' catches the outward act and loses the lie in it; YLT 'feign obedience' is nearer. The enemies bow, but the bow is a fraud born of terror, which Metzudat David and Radak read as their claiming they had never hated.

The last clause is the knot. 'Their time' can mean the enemies' appointed time, their doom, that endures for ever, as Rashi and Malbim read it, or Israel's time of blessing that would have lasted for ever, as Radak and Metzudat David read it. The KJV chose the first ('their time should have endured for ever') without noting the other. Play it with an ominous finality, but let the doubt sit.

philological_notes.note: Piel of 'lie, deny, deceive'. With the preposition ל it describes cringing, feigned obedience from fear. Ibn Ezra compares it with Deut 33:29 and Ps 66:3.
'Their time', ambiguous: the enemies' doom (Rashi, Malbim) or the time of blessing for Israel (Radak, Metzudat David).

verses.translation_literal: And he fed him from the fat of wheat, and from a rock, honey I will satisfy you.
verses.translation_dramatic: He would feed him on the very fat of the wheat. And from the rock itself, honey: with that I would fill you to the full.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends in food, the oldest language of blessing. 'The fat of wheat' (חלב חטה) is not an oily grain but the best of the harvest, the marrow of the kernel, as 'the fat of the land' (Gen 45:18) is the best of the land. Wheat was the grain of the well-off; barley was the poor man's bread. Honey from a rock is the wilderness miracle remembered in Deut 32:13: sweetness where there should be stone. The promise is that obedience would turn even barren places into feasts.

Note the grammar, which the KJV smooths over. The verse begins in the third person ('he fed him') and ends in the second ('I satisfy you'): God speaks of himself as 'he', then as 'I'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri treat this as the ordinary prophetic shift of voice. The KJV makes the whole conditional ('should have fed them... should I have satisfied thee'), which is the sense, but the Hebrew has an open ending, with a future 'I will satisfy you', on which the last word hangs.

philological_notes.note: 'The fat of wheat': the best, the choicest. Metzudat Zion compares 'the fat of the land' (Gen 45:18).
'Honey from a rock', recalling 'he made him suck honey from the crag' (Deut 32:13), as Rashi and Metzudat David note. Radak takes it as a figure for the wealth of conquered fortresses.
